strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: extrapolating dynamic 3D Gaussian scenes beyond the observed time window, rather than only reconstructing/interpolating training frames.

The proposed design is conceptually coherent: augment Gaussians with a latent dynamics state, encode local/global particle features, evolve the global latent state with a Neural ODE, and decode time-conditioned affine Gaussian deformations.

The experimental section includes several relevant baselines across reconstruction-focused methods and extrapolation methods, with results on both synthetic NVFi datasets and a real PanopticSports benchmark.

The reported synthetic extrapolation gains are substantial in many cases, especially on Dynamic Objects and Dynamic Indoor Scene, suggesting the method can capture predictable motion patterns better than standard dynamic reconstruction models.
The paper includes useful ablations showing that removing the latent dynamics state severely hurts performance, and that the ODE and affine decoder provide additional gains.
weaknesses: The central claim that the method learns underlying dynamics or differential equations is overstated. The Neural ODE appears to evolve only a global latent vector while local particle features remain fixed, and there is no evidence that the learned ODE corresponds to interpretable or physically meaningful dynamics rather than a smooth time-conditioned latent model.

The real-world evidence is much less convincing than the synthetic evidence. On PanopticSports, gains over GaussianPrediction are small in PSNR/SSIM, LPIPS is often worse, and several baselines used in the synthetic experiments are omitted, limiting the strength of the generalization claim.

The extrapolation setting is relatively narrow: predictions are evaluated on short held-out future intervals from the same scene, with predictable motion. The paper does not test longer-horizon drift, multimodal futures, abrupt action changes, or cross-scene generalization, despite emphasizing prior-free motion prediction.

The ablation results partially weaken the main methodological argument: removing the Neural ODE or affine deformation causes only modest drops compared with the full model, while the catastrophic 'w/o latent space' variant may not be a fair isolated ablation of the proposed dynamics mechanism.

Reproducibility is incomplete. Important implementation details are missing or vague, including latent dimensions, number of FPS centers/neighborhoods, Gaussian initialization, ODE integration step settings, optimizer details, random seeds, and exact baseline training protocols. The abstract says code is available but gives no actual URL.

Some technical and presentation issues reduce confidence: the probabilistic problem formulation is not well justified, the training objective appears to involve future ground-truth sequences despite the train/test split, several table entries are poorly formatted or suspicious, and terms such as 'prior-free', 'physically plausible', and 'learned dynamical laws' are used more strongly than the evidence supports.

strengths: The paper targets an important and underexplored problem: extrapolating dynamic 3D Gaussian scenes beyond the observed time window, rather than only reconstructing/interpolating the training sequence.

The proposed pipeline is coherent at a high level: augment Gaussians with latent dynamics, encode local/global features, evolve the global latent state with a Neural ODE, and decode affine Gaussian deformations.

The evaluation includes relevant dynamic extrapolation benchmarks, including NVFi synthetic object/indoor datasets and PanopticSports, and compares against both reconstruction-oriented 4D methods and extrapolation-oriented baselines such as NVFi and GaussianPrediction.
The reported extrapolation numbers on the NVFi datasets are often substantially better than the baselines, suggesting the method may be practically useful for some predictable motions.
weaknesses: The core novelty is weaker than claimed. The method is largely a combination of hash/local features, PointNet/Transformer-style global encoding, Neural ODE latent evolution, and Gaussian deformation decoding. The paper repeatedly frames this as learning physical particle dynamics, but the model only evolves a learned global latent vector and does not establish that the learned ODE corresponds to meaningful dynamics.

The ablation study undermines the importance of several proposed components. Removing the Neural ODE or affine deformation causes only modest drops relative to the full model in Table 4, while the large drop from removing the latent space is not very diagnostic because that likely removes most of the deformation capacity. This makes it hard to attribute the gains to the claimed dynamics formulation.

Experimental evidence is too narrow for the strength of the claims. The method is evaluated mostly on predictable short-horizon sequences; there is no stress test on longer horizons, stochastic or multimodal future motion, out-of-distribution dynamics, different training-window lengths, or genuinely ambiguous futures. The paper claims general prior-free extrapolation but only demonstrates deterministic continuation on limited benchmarks.

The PanopticSports results are mixed. ParticleGS is only marginally better than GaussianPrediction in PSNR/SSIM on several extrapolation cases and often worse in LPIPS, yet the paper presents the results as broadly superior. The real-world evidence therefore does not strongly support the claimed advantage.

The comparison protocol is insufficiently documented. It is unclear whether all baselines were re-tuned under comparable settings, how sensitive results are to split choices, and whether all methods use the same training views, optimization budgets, and model capacity. Since extrapolation metrics can be strongly affected by reconstruction quality and dataset sparsity, this matters materially.

Reproducibility is weak. The abstract says code is available but no link is provided. Important implementation details are missing or vague, including hash encoding resolutions, FPS/KNN counts, ODE solver step settings, architecture specifics for the decoders, initialization, densification schedule interactions, random seeds, and training/runtime cost beyond the GPU type.

The formulation and writing contain technical and presentation issues that reduce confidence: the objective notation is confused, Figure 2 is referenced as Figure 4.1, the method sometimes says it learns equations from video while only optimizing photometric rendering losses, and the paper uses overstated language such as 'no need to manually define priors' despite using architectural priors such as affine deformation and global latent evolution.

The paper does not address failure cases or limitations deeply. It acknowledges lack of generalization/pretraining, but does not analyze when the learned dynamics fails, how errors accumulate over time, or whether the model simply extrapolates smooth temporal trends rather than learning robust scene dynamics.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and relatively under-served problem: extrapolating dynamic 3D scenes beyond observed frames, rather than only reconstructing/interpolating known time ranges.

The core idea is coherent and useful: augmenting 3D Gaussians with a latent dynamics state, evolving a global latent state with a Neural ODE, and decoding latent states into Gaussian deformations provides a clean framework for continuous-time motion extrapolation without hand-specified physical equations.

The empirical results are broadly strong. On the NVFi Dynamic Object and Dynamic Indoor Scene benchmarks, ParticleGS substantially improves extrapolation PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS over reconstruction-oriented 3DGS baselines and over prior extrapolation methods such as NVFi and GaussianPrediction in most scenes.

The paper includes relevant comparisons across NeRF-based dynamic methods, 3DGS reconstruction methods, physics-informed extrapolation, and graph-based extrapolation, which helps position the contribution clearly.

Ablations support the main design direction: removing the latent dynamics space causes a large degradation, and removing the ODE module or affine deformation decoder also reduces extrapolation performance.
The method remains competitive in reconstruction quality while improving extrapolation, which is valuable because the paper does not trade away the standard dynamic rendering objective entirely.
weaknesses: The claim of being "prior-free" is somewhat overstated. The method avoids explicit physical equations and manually specified forces, but it still embeds strong architectural priors through global latent evolution, affine deformation decoding, neighborhood grouping, and RK4 ODE integration.

The evaluation breadth is good but not fully convincing for a general extrapolation method. Most of the strongest gains are on NVFi synthetic/indoor benchmarks; on PanopticSports the gains over GaussianPrediction are modest, mixed across metrics, and only a subset of baselines is reported.

The extrapolation setup could be clearer and more rigorously justified. The paper notes that extrapolation metrics can sometimes exceed reconstruction metrics because of sparse novel views, which complicates interpretation of the reported train/test split and makes it harder to isolate motion prediction quality from view synthesis difficulty.

The ablation study is useful but limited. The latent-state ablation is decisive, but the ODE and affine-deformation ablations show relatively small average gains on NVFi, so the evidence for each individual module is weaker than the paper's narrative suggests.

The method learns a single likely future trajectory and does not address multimodality or uncertainty in future motion, despite formulating the task probabilistically. This is acceptable for short-term extrapolation but limits the strength of claims about general future prediction.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the manuscript: implementation details are partial, important hyperparameters such as latent dimensions/group sizes are not fully specified, runtime and memory costs are not reported, and the abstract's code URL appears blank.

The presentation has several polish issues, including inconsistent spelling of ParticleGS/ParticalGS, grammatical errors, and some overclaiming about learning dynamics equations or physical plausibility without direct physical validation. These do not undermine the main contribution but should be corrected.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: future extrapolation for dynamic 3D Gaussian scenes, where standard time-conditioned deformation models often interpolate well but extrapolate poorly.

The proposed encoder-evolver-decoder formulation is technically coherent. Factorizing per-Gaussian static features from shared latent dynamic fields is a sensible design that reduces ODE evolution cost while still allowing per-particle deformations through the decoder.

The experimental results are broad for this subarea, covering synthetic object, indoor, multipart, and real-world GoPro datasets. ParticleGS consistently improves extrapolation PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS over time-conditioned, physics-prior, and velocity-field baselines in the aggregate tables.

The ablation study is useful: removing the Neural ODE evolver, physical decoding, progressive training, or neighborhood regularization each degrades performance, supporting that the main architectural choices matter.

The appendix provides meaningful implementation details, per-scene quantitative results, and additional qualitative comparisons, improving transparency relative to many dynamic 3D reconstruction papers.
weaknesses: The central framing as learning 'physical laws' is stronger than the evidence supports. The method learns a latent continuous-time dynamical system optimized for photometric rendering, but no physical quantities, conservation properties, force laws, or physical plausibility metrics are validated. The Neural ODE could still be fitting smooth latent trajectories rather than discovering scene physics.

The extrapolation setting is relatively constrained: training uses the first 75% of each sequence and testing uses the remaining 25%. This demonstrates within-sequence future prediction, but not robustness to longer horizons, abrupt events, changed forces, different initial conditions, or unseen scenes. The stated physical-world understanding claims therefore feel overextended.

The real-world improvements are modest. On FreeGave-GoPro, the average extrapolation gain over FreeGave is small in PSNR, and per-scene results show losses or near ties on Wrist Rest and Hammer. The strongest claims are mainly supported by synthetic datasets.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The appendix gives architecture and iteration counts, but important details such as learning rates, optimizer hyperparameters, loss weights, densification/pruning schedules, ODE step settings, random seeds, and exact baseline reproduction protocols are not fully specified.

The comparison fairness is hard to assess from the manuscript alone. Baselines span different assumptions and may require careful tuning for extrapolation; the paper states they are run on a single GPU but does not provide enough configuration detail to judge whether each baseline was optimized comparably.

Some analysis is conceptually oversimplified. The toy oscillator experiment contrasts a weak time-to-position baseline with a Neural ODE and does not isolate the proposed 3DGS-specific factorization; it mainly illustrates a known advantage of state-space dynamics rather than proving ParticleGS learns physical dynamics from video.

The method's limitations are under-discussed. The global shared dynamic field design may struggle with scenes containing multiple independent interactions, contact discontinuities, topology changes, or new external impulses, but these failure modes are not experimentally explored.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: future extrapolation for dynamic 3D Gaussian scenes, where standard time-conditioned reconstruction methods are known to be weak.

The proposed Encoder-Evolver-Decoder structure is coherent and practically motivated. Factorizing per-Gaussian static features from shared latent dynamic fields is a reasonable way to reduce the cost of ODE-based evolution.

The experiments cover several relevant datasets, including synthetic object/indoor/multipart scenes and a real-world GoPro dataset, and compare against both reconstruction-oriented and physics/dynamics-oriented baselines such as NVFi, TRACE, and FreeGave.

The reported quantitative results are often strong, especially on synthetic extrapolation benchmarks, and the ablations provide some evidence that the Neural ODE evolver, physical decoding, progressive training, and neighborhood updates contribute to performance.
weaknesses: The central claim that the method learns physical laws is not well supported. The Neural ODE evolves unconstrained latent fields with no conservation laws, equivariance, contact/friction modeling, force inference, or validation of physical quantities. The evidence mainly shows improved image-space extrapolation, not learned physics.

The technical formulation is under-justified. Broadcasting the same global dynamic fields to all Gaussians and relying on static per-particle features plus an MLP decoder does not clearly model particle interactions or local physical state evolution. The Markov/physical-state argument is asserted rather than demonstrated.

The decoder equation is ambiguous and possibly problematic: x_t = x + Rod(R)x + T appears to add both the original position and its rotated version, rather than applying a standard rigid transform or displacement. This raises concerns about the claimed physically meaningful decoding.

The evaluation does not convincingly separate true dynamics learning from sequence-specific curve fitting. Training on the first 75% and testing on the last 25% of the same sequences is useful, but the paper lacks longer-horizon extrapolation, stress tests, perturbations, cross-scene generalization, or cases with changed initial conditions.

Some empirical claims are overstated. On the real-world FreeGave-GoPro dataset, the improvement over FreeGave is modest in PSNR, and reconstruction quality is essentially comparable. The statement of large improvements across all datasets is not consistently supported by the tables.

Baseline fairness and reproducibility are not fully convincing. The manuscript does not provide enough detail on baseline tuning, identical training budgets, code availability, random seeds, variance, or whether the newer baselines were rerun faithfully under the same split and resolution.

The ablation replacing the ODE with an MLP is underspecified, so it is hard to know whether the gain comes from continuous-time dynamics, parameterization, training schedule, solver behavior, or simply a stronger inductive bias for the chosen benchmark split.

The paper’s presentation repeatedly uses strong physical language, but the method is closer to a latent continuous deformation model. This overclaiming is a material weakness because it affects interpretation of the contribution, not just wording.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: extrapolating dynamic 3D Gaussian scenes beyond the observed video window, rather than only interpolating/reconstructing seen times. This is a meaningful computer vision contribution with clear relevance to physical world modeling and dynamic novel-view synthesis.

The proposed Encoder-Evolver-Decoder design is coherent and technically interesting. Factoring each scene into per-particle static features and shared dynamic fields, then evolving those fields with a Neural ODE, is a plausible way to reduce state dimensionality while encouraging temporal consistency.

The empirical evidence is fairly broad. The paper evaluates on Dynamic Object, Dynamic Indoor Scene, Dynamic Multipart, and FreeGave-GoPro, and compares against time-conditioned methods, physics-prior methods, and recent velocity-field approaches. Reported extrapolation gains are substantial on several synthetic benchmarks and still positive on the real GoPro data.

The ablations are useful and generally support the design choices: removing the ODE evolver, physical decoding, progressive training, neighborhood regularization, or reducing the number of dynamic fields degrades extrapolation performance.

The manuscript is mostly clear, with a readable problem formulation, architecture diagrams, qualitative comparisons, full per-scene supplementary tables, and implementation details such as network sizes, training schedule, ODE solver, and physical-state dimensions.
weaknesses: The paper sometimes overclaims that the method learns “physical laws.” The learned latent ODE improves extrapolation, but there is little direct evidence that the latent fields correspond to true physical quantities or obey physically meaningful conservation/causal constraints. The RGB latent-state visualization is suggestive but not sufficient to establish physical interpretability.

The technical formulation has a potential inconsistency in the decoder equation: x_t = x + Rod(R)x + T appears to add both the original position and the rotated position, which would not reduce to the identity transform under zero rotation unless Rod(R) is defined as a residual rotation offset. This should be clarified, as it affects the claimed physically meaningful motion factorization.

The extrapolation setting is limited to training on the first 75% of frames and testing on the remaining 25%. This is a reasonable benchmark protocol, but it does not fully stress long-horizon stability, out-of-distribution events, contacts, topology changes, or interventions. The limitation section only briefly acknowledges sudden behavior changes.

The factorized global dynamic-field design is efficient, but its expressive limits are not deeply analyzed. Since the same evolved fields are broadcast to all Gaussians and particle specificity enters through static features and decoding, it is unclear how well the approach scales to scenes with many independent interacting objects or localized dynamics.

Some experimental claims would benefit from stronger fairness and reproducibility detail. The paper says baselines are run on a single RTX 4090, but does not provide enough detail on baseline tuning, checkpoint/source versions, or whether all methods use identical data preprocessing and splits. No variance or repeated-run stability is reported.

The ablation for removing factorized encoding is incomplete: it is run only on Dynamic Object and on a different A6000 GPU, and the table does not report the actual memory/time cost that motivates the design. This weakens the evidence for the efficiency argument.

On the real-world FreeGave-GoPro dataset, the gains over TRACE/FreeGave are modest, and reconstruction quality is essentially tied. This does not undermine the paper, but it tempers the strength of the acceptance case compared with the larger synthetic improvements.
